title: The Bike Workshop
transcript:
A: Today I'm talking to Delia Marsh, who runs a bike repair workshop in Larkfield. Delia, you started out in a garage, didn't you?
B: That's right. Well, a shed, actually. My dad's old shed behind the house. I fixed bikes for the neighbours, mostly for free, to be honest.
A: And when did it become a real business?
B: About six years ago. A man brought in a very old racing bike and offered to pay me forty pounds. I thought, hang on, people will actually pay for this! So I rented a small shop.
A: Was it easy?
B: Not at all. The first winter was terrible. Nobody cycles when it's raining, and I nearly closed in February.
A: What changed?
B: I started running evening classes. Simple things, like how to mend a puncture. I expected five or six people. Thirty came!
A: Thirty!
B: Yes, and most of them then bought their spare parts from me, so the classes paid for themselves. Now they're the most important part of the business, more than the repairs, if I'm honest.
A: Would you ever open a second shop?
B: People ask me that all the time. I don't think so. I like knowing everyone who walks in. If I had two shops, I'd be driving between them all day, and I'd lose the part I enjoy most.
A: So what's next?
B: A repair course for teenagers. The council might help with the cost, but we'll see.

title: Rethinking the High Street
transcript:
Okay, let's move on to how small changes in a street can change what people do. I'll use an imaginary example, so please don't go looking for it in the library.

Imagine a town called Brenmouth. Its high street has heavy traffic, narrow pavements, and most shoppers just hurry through. Now, the council has two options. Option one: widen the road to reduce queues. Option two: widen the pavements and add benches and trees.

Most people's first instinct, I think, is option one. Less traffic, more customers, right? But look at what tends to happen. When a road is wider, cars go faster, and fewer people feel like stopping. With wider pavements, everything slows down. Drivers take more care, and pedestrians feel safer.

Here's the interesting part. In our imaginary case, the shop owners were worried at first, because they'd lose a few parking spaces. However, after a year, the shops reported more customers, not fewer, and people were staying twice as long on average.

Now, I want to be careful. One example doesn't prove a rule. Many other things could explain it, such as the weather, or a new café opening. But the idea is worth taking seriously. And that leads me to my second point: how do we actually measure whether a street is working?

title: The Library of Tools
transcript:
A: In the town of Wexley, there's a library where you can't borrow a single book. Well, that's not quite true. But I'm here at the Wexley Toolshare, where you can borrow a drill, a ladder, or even a sewing machine. I'm with the manager, Ravi. Ravi, how did this start?

A: And what's the most popular item?

A: What's the biggest challenge?

title: The Case for Napping
transcript:
A: My guest today is Dr Imogen Falk, a sleep researcher, whose team recently published a small study on napping. Imogen, welcome. Before we begin, I should say I've been a devoted napper for years, so I'm hoping you're going to tell me I was right all along.
B: Ha, well, I'm afraid it's not quite that simple.
A: Oh dear.
B: So, what we did, and I should stress this was a modest study, only sixty participants, was to give half of them a nap of twenty minutes after lunch, timed meticulously, and the other half no nap, and then compare their performance on memory tasks.
A: And the sleepers did better.
B: At first glance, yes, by a fair margin. But here's the catch. When we looked more closely, the effect was strongest in people who normally sleep badly at night. For those who sleep well, the difference was negligible.
A: So napping is a kind of repair, rather than a bonus.
B: That's a plausible way of putting it, although I'd be wary of drawing that conclusion too firmly. Sixty people is not many, and they were all university staff, which isn't exactly a typical group.
A: Right. But surely there's no harm in a nap?
B: Not necessarily harm, no. Though we did notice that some participants who napped for longer than half an hour woke up feeling dull, and actually performed worse than those who didn't nap at all. So timing matters. It's not a case of the more, the better.
A: Which rather spoils my plan for a whole afternoon asleep.
B: I'm afraid it does, yes. But if you're short on sleep, twenty minutes is probably a sensible compromise. Whether it works for everyone, we can't say yet. That's the honest answer.

title: Should Museums Charge?
transcript:
A: So, to our final topic tonight: should public museums charge for entry? Dana, you've written a lot about this.
B: I have, and I'll be candid, I used to think free entry was untouchable. But I've reluctantly changed my mind, partly. Not completely.
C: Really? I'm surprised, Dana.
B: Well, hear me out. The cost of looking after a collection keeps rising, and when funding falls short, it's the education programmes that get cut first, not the exhibitions. I'd rather charge visitors a few pounds than lose the school workshops.
C: But that's a false choice, surely. Once you put up a ticket desk, you send a message about who the place is for, and you risk alienating the very people you most want. Families on a tight budget simply won't come. They'll think, not for us.
B: That's a fair worry. But isn't there a middle path? Free for children, free for local residents, and a charge for tourists.
C: In theory, yes. In practice, you need staff to check who's local, which eats into the money you've raised. A gallery I know of, which I won't name, ended up spending almost a third of its ticket income on checking.
A: So is that an argument against charging, or just against clever schemes?
C: Both, I'd say. Keep it simple: free for everyone, and ask for donations at the door.
B: Donations? That rarely covers the gap, in my experience. People say they'll give, then walk straight past the box.
C: Maybe. But I'd still prefer to fall short with free entry than succeed with a barrier.
A: Strong words. Dana, last thought?
B: I'd say we're both defending the same goal. We just disagree about the risk.

title: The Sunk Cost Trap
transcript:
Right, last week we talked about how people fall in love with their own plans. Today I'd like to look at a related trap, one that economists call the sunk cost effect. Let me set up a hypothetical, entirely fictional case.

Imagine a company, Norvale Foods, which has spent three years and several million pounds developing a new frozen dessert. Just before launch, test results come in, and they're disappointing. Customers like it, but not enough to justify the production costs. What should the managers do?

Logically, the money already spent is gone whatever they decide, so the only question should be: from here on, does the product pay for itself? If not, stop. But that's rarely what happens. Typically, someone says, we've come this far, we can't walk away now. And that sounds like determination, doesn't it? Except it's really a way of avoiding the discomfort of admitting a mistake. Hindsight makes it look obvious, but at the time, walking away feels daunting.

Now, I don't want to suggest that persistence is always foolish. There are plenty of projects that looked hopeless in year two and turned out well in year five. The difficulty, inherent in the whole problem, is telling the two situations apart. One rule of thumb I find helpful is to ask whether you would start the project today, knowing what you now know. If the answer is no, then continuing needs a much better reason than, we've already paid for it.

A colleague of mine goes further and says organisations should appoint someone whose job is to argue for stopping the project. I'm not convinced that works; people tend to ignore the official critic. But the principle behind it, that we need some check against our own stubbornness, is sound. Next time, we'll look at how group dynamics make this even worse.

title: Late to the Violin
transcript:
I started the violin at forty three, which, I'll admit, was a slightly ridiculous thing to do. My daughter had been learning for a year, and I'd listen from the kitchen thinking, how hard can it be? Quite hard, as it turns out, and daunting too. I am not accustomed to being bad at things. For the first three months I produced a noise that made the cat leave the house.

Now, people often assume that the biggest obstacle for adult learners is time. Between work and family, who has an hour a day? But in my experience, that isn't really it. You can get a lot done in fifteen minutes if you're focused. The real obstacle is pride. Children don't mind sounding terrible. They squeal, they laugh, they carry on. Adults hear every wrong note and take it personally. I was close to giving up in the spring, after a lesson where the teacher, very kindly, asked me to play just a little more quietly. I understood exactly what she intended.

What helped me continue, oddly enough, was not talent or discipline. It was a retired plumber in my class, seventy years old, who played worse than I did and absolutely didn't care. He'd finish a piece, grin, and say, well, that was an adventure. And I thought, why am I so afraid of being bad at something that doesn't matter?

So I stopped aiming for perfect. I started recording myself once a week, not to criticise, just to notice small changes. It's slow progress, and I won't pretend I'm good. But last month I played a simple tune at my daughter's birthday, and nobody left the room. For me, that counts as a triumph.

title: Translating Humour
transcript:
A: I'm joined by Ottilie Brandt, who has worked for thirty years translating comic novels, which strikes me as either the best job in the world or a kind of slow torture. Which is it?
B: Both, depending on the week. People assume the hard part is vocabulary, but I'm meticulous about words, and vocabulary is almost never the problem. A pun is a different matter. You can't carry it across, so you have to decide what to sacrifice.
A: The meaning or the joke?
B: That's the textbook question, and I used to answer it with, the meaning, always. These days I'm less certain. If the author's pun is the whole point of the paragraph, then keeping the sense and losing the laugh is a kind of betrayal, isn't it? It's accurate, and it's dead.
A: So you invent a new joke.
B: Sometimes. Though not lightly. There's a fine line between adaptation and showing off. I once translated a character's terrible pun about a fish and, frankly, my replacement was cleverer than the original. The editor adored it. I didn't, because it sounded like me, not the author.
A: Did you keep it?
B: I cut it. I'm not sentimental about my own sentences. Which, now I say it aloud, probably made the book slightly less funny. But there are things you owe to the writer.
A: Do readers notice?
B: Rarely, and that's rather the point. If I've done it well, nobody is aware of me at all. The odd thing is that praise for a translation can be a warning sign. Readers admire the beautiful language, when the original was deliberately plain. There's a question of authenticity here: the author's voice has to survive. In other words, I've interfered.
A: So disappearing is the goal?
B: Mostly. Although I'd be lying if I said I never wanted a little credit. Everyone does. We simply become adept at hiding it.
A: Last question. Would you ever write your own comic novel?
B: I've been threatening to for years. The trouble is that I know exactly how hard it is. I'd probably spend a decade rewriting the first page, and then, I suspect, someone would translate it badly.

title: Why Forecasts Fail
transcript:
I'd like to start today with a study that, I should say at once, is invented. I've constructed it to illustrate a pattern that real researchers have described in various forms, and I don't want anyone quoting my numbers.

Imagine a panel of two hundred forecasters, economists, analysts, commentators, each asked to predict a hundred events over five years. And imagine that we score them. What do we find? First, as a group, they perform only slightly better than chance. That in itself isn't shocking. The surprise is in who does worst. It's not the cautious ones. It's the confident ones, the people with one big theory, held with unwavering conviction, that explains everything. They're also, tellingly, the ones most often invited onto television.

Now, why? One explanation is that a single big idea makes a plausible story, and stories are persuasive, to the audience and, crucially, to the forecaster. Once you have a premise you love, every new fact seems to fit it, and hindsight makes the fit look inevitable. The other kind of forecaster, who is adept at changing course, borrows from many theories, hedges, and revises. They sound less impressive. They say, it depends, rather a lot. But they get more right.

Now, here comes the complication, and I want to flag it before you leave thinking that hedging is a virtue in itself. A forecaster who says everything is possible can never be wrong, and can never be useful either. The skill lies in calibration: saying seventy per cent when things happen about seven times in ten. That is far harder than either bold certainty or comfortable vagueness.

And I'd add one more thing, which is slightly uncomfortable for those of us who teach. Training people in the theories, as we do, doesn't obviously help. It may even encourage the one-big-idea habit. I haven't resolved that tension, and I'm not sure I can.

title: The Clock Mender

speakers.label: B
speakers.voice: man, 60s, clock repairer, gentle, neutral British

transcript:
A: In a tiny workshop above a bakery in the fictional town of Marlow Down, there's a sound I can only describe as a hundred small arguments, ticking. That's the sound of Hugo Seaton's clocks. Hugo, do they ever agree with each other?
B: Never. Not for long. Some run fast in the morning, slow by evening. It's the temperature, mainly. A clock is a very honest, resilient instrument. It tells you everything about the room it's in.
A: You repair them for a living, but you tell me business is poor.
B: Poor isn't quite the word. It's odd, actually. More people than ever bring me clocks, but nearly all of them want one just to look handsome. People call it nostalgia, but I'm not sure. Wound up and left silent on a shelf. They don't want it to work.
A: And that bothers you.
B: I'm not sure bothers is right. At first it did. I thought, what is the point of a clock that doesn't keep time? But then a woman came in with an old clock from her grandfather, and she told me, I do not need it to be right, I need to hear it. And I saw what she meant. It had stopped being a tool and become a kind of company.
A: So the function has changed.
B: Has it? Perhaps the function was always a bit more than telling the time. Nobody needed a clock to be accurate to the second until railways and factories demanded it. Before that, church bells did the job well enough.
A: Do you worry about who will take over?
B: Constantly. I've had two apprentices, and both left within a year. One explained, quite politely, that he couldn't spend his life on something a phone does better.
A: What did you say?
B: I said he was right. And then I told him to come back the day his phone became good company.
A: Ha! Did he come back?
B: Not yet. I haven't given up hope. It's an antiquated trade, I know, and tenacity is rather the whole of it. Meticulous patience, you see. You sit with a stubborn little mechanism for days, and one morning, it simply starts to beat.

title: Stand in the Rain

speakers.label: A
speakers.voice: man, 60s, retiring engineer, warm, neutral British

transcript:
Thank you, all of you. Please sit down, I haven't said anything yet, and you may not want to stand once I have. I was asked to say a few words about what I've learned in thirty eight years of building bridges, and I've spent the last week trying to decide whether I've learned anything at all.

The honest answer is: one thing, really, and I learned it by getting it wrong. Early in my career, I designed a bridge for pedestrians, nothing grand, across a river in a town I won't name. On paper it was perfect. Efficient, elegant, cheap, and meticulously checked. And the day it opened, I was there feeling rather pleased with myself, with an unwavering belief in my own drawings, until I noticed that people were refusing to use it. They walked two hundred metres up the river and crossed by the old road. I was puzzled.

Eventually, a woman with a baby explained, with great patience, that the ramp was steeper than it looked, and the railing was freezing in winter. Nobody had told me, because nobody had asked her.

In hindsight, it was a humbling lesson. Now, I'd love to say I changed overnight. In fact, it took me years to take it in. We engineers are trained to trust calculation, and calculation is wonderful, but it only answers the questions you've thought to ask. What I eventually understood is that the most important measurements can't be taken in an office. They're taken by standing in the rain and watching what people actually do.

So, to the younger engineers here: go and stand in the rain. And to the older ones: stop pretending you don't need to.

I'll miss this place more than I'm letting on. I've been told I'm not allowed to say I'll be back on Monday, so I'll say instead that I'll be back for the cake. Thank you.

title: The Cost of Noise
transcript:
Good afternoon. I want to talk about something we've all stopped hearing, which is, of course, the problem. City noise. Now, when I raise this with colleagues, the response is usually a polite shrug. Noise is annoying, they say, but surely not serious.

So let me begin with a small, fictional experiment, one I'd love to run if anybody gave me the funding. Take two streets with the same traffic, the same air quality, the same rents. On one, the buildings are lined with soft planting; on the other, hard glass and concrete. Over a year, and with meticulous care, we measure not hearing but behaviour: how long people sit outside, how often neighbours stop to talk, how many leave. My hypothesis, and it is only a hypothesis, is that the quieter street will look healthier in ways nobody put on the survey, with fewer adverse effects on neighbourliness.

Why do I suspect so? Because noise doesn't merely irritate; it taxes attention. Every sound you try to ignore uses a little effort, and effort accumulates, amid the din, into something tedious and draining. By evening you aren't exhausted from anything you did, just from everything you didn't listen to.

Now, the obvious fix is volume: make things quieter. And in some cases that's right, and it can alleviate real suffering. But I've come to think it's the wrong first question. A busy fountain makes more noise than a distant motorway, yet nobody complains about the fountain. So perhaps the real issue isn't loudness but control and meaning; whether a sound is one you chose, or one that's imposed.

I realise that this complicates policy. It's far easier to set a decibel limit than to measure how people feel. But easy to measure and important are rarely the same thing, and I'd rather be roughly right about the second than precisely right about the first. In the time left, I'll walk through three design changes that cost almost nothing and, I'd argue, matter a great deal.
